workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on appearance
Watchful waiting -- most resolve spontaneously within 6-18 months
Physical removal (curettage or cryotherapy) if lesions are troublesome or cosmetically bothersome
Consider an immunosuppression/HIV work-up if lesions are unusually extensive, large, or persistent, particularly in an adult

exam.step: Inspect the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds and behind the ears for greasy, yellowish scale on mild redness
exam.positive: The classic distribution and appearance

exam.step: Ask about a waxing/waning course with stress or seasonal triggers
exam.positive: A relapsing-remitting pattern is typical, distinguishing it from a one-off acute rash

exam.step: Ask about the extent and treatment-resistance, especially in an adult
exam.positive: Unusually severe or resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis can be a marker of underlying immunosuppression

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient given the characteristic distribution and appearance
Reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain presentations

conditions.name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Greasy, yellowish scaling on a mildly red base, classically on the scalp, eyebrows, sides of the nose and behind the ears -- a chronic, relapsing-remitting condition linked to an inflammatory reaction to Malassezia yeast naturally living on the skin, not a true infection. Flares are often triggered by stress, cold weather, or reduced skin care. Mild hair thinning can occur over affected scalp areas. Widespread, unusually severe or treatment-resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis, especially in an adult, can be a marker of underlying immunosuppression (including undiagnosed HIV) and should prompt that consideration.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on appearance and distribution
Topical antifungal (ketoconazole or ciclopirox) shampoo/cream
Topical mild corticosteroid for flares
Regular, ongoing use of medicated shampoo to prevent recurrence -- this is a chronic, relapsing condition, not a one-off cure

exam.step: Inspect for well-defined, milky-white patches, checking under Wood's lamp if available
exam.positive: Wood's lamp examination confirms and defines the true extent of depigmentation

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the patches itch, hurt, or have any scale
exam.positive: Vitiligo is classically asymptomatic -- genuine itch, pain or scale should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis

exam.step: Ask about a family or personal history of autoimmune conditions, especially thyroid disease
exam.positive: Vitiligo is genuinely associated with other autoimmune conditions, particularly autoimmune thyroid disease

labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis and defines the true extent of depigmented skin
Screens for the genuinely associated autoimmune thyroid disease

conditions.name: Vitiligo

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Well-defined, milky-white patches of skin caused by loss of pigment-producing melanocytes -- classically asymptomatic (no itch, pain or scale), slowly progressive, and often starting around the hands, face, or body folds. An autoimmune-associated condition, not infectious or contagious -- an important reassurance point, since the visible appearance is often mistaken by patients or others for a contagious skin infection. Rapidly changing pigment loss, or pigment loss with genuine itch/scale, should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis rather than assuming vitiligo.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on appearance
Wood's lamp examination to confirm and define extent
Screen for associated autoimmune conditions (thyroid disease in particular)
Topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors
Phototherapy (narrowband UVB) for more extensive disease

exam.step: Inspect for a pearly/waxy bump, a persistent scaly patch, or a sore that bleeds and doesn't heal, on sun-exposed skin
exam.positive: The classic pattern -- warrants prompt assessment rather than reassurance

exam.step: Ask specifically how long the lesion has been present and whether it has changed, bled, or failed to heal
exam.positive: Slow growth over months to years with bleeding or non-healing is the concerning pattern, distinct from an acute infection

exam.step: Assess sun-exposure history and skin type
exam.positive: Cumulative sun exposure and fair skin are the dominant risk factors, especially in older adults

labs.confirms: Aids clinical diagnosis and helps decide which lesions need biopsy
Definitive diagnosis for any clinically suspicious lesion -- should not be delayed

conditions.name: Skin cancer (non-melanoma)

triage.label: Urgent
triage.action: Seek medical assessment today

conditions.summary: A slow-growing, often painless skin lesion -- a pearly or waxy bump, a persistent scaly patch, or a sore that bleeds easily and doesn't fully heal -- developing over months to years, usually on sun-exposed skin (face, ears, scalp, hands) in older adults. Actinic keratosis (rough, scaly, sun-damage patches) is a precursor that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma if untreated. Any new or changing skin lesion in this pattern -- especially one that bleeds, doesn't heal, or is enlarging -- needs prompt clinical assessment and often a biopsy, not reassurance or watchful waiting.
workup: Prompt clinical assessment -- do not delay for a lesion matching this pattern
Dermoscopy
Biopsy of any clinically suspicious lesion
Surgical excision or other definitive treatment once confirmed, per the specific diagnosis and risk category

exam.step: Look inside the cheeks for Koplik's spots (tiny white-grey spots on a red background)
exam.positive: The single most specific early sign, present in 60-70% of cases -- no dedicated evidence node captures this directly, so it is assessed visually

exam.step: Confirm the classic sequence: fever and the '3 Cs' (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) preceding the rash by 2-4 days
exam.positive: This sequence, and the rash spreading from the face downward, is the classic pattern

exam.step: Check vaccination status and any known exposure/outbreak
exam.positive: Measles occurs almost exclusively in unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals

labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis, particularly important given its notifiable-disease and public-health status
Often sufficient in a known outbreak with the classic clinical picture

conditions.name: Measles

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: A highly contagious viral illness starting with high fever, cough, runny nose and conjunctivitis (the classic '3 Cs') 2-4 days before a red-brown, blotchy rash spreads from the face down the body. Koplik's spots -- tiny white-grey spots on the inside of the cheeks -- are the single most specific early sign but appear in only 60-70% of cases and are not captured by a dedicated evidence node here, so this is assessed on examination. Occurs in unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals of any age, not just children. Serious complications (pneumonia, encephalitis) are genuinely more common than in most other childhood exanthems, so this should never be dismissed as 'just a rash'.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis, supported by measles IgM/PCR testing
Notify public health -- measles is a notifiable disease in most jurisdictions
Supportive care (fluids, antipyretics)
Vitamin A supplementation per WHO guidance, which reduces complication severity
Isolation until 4 days after rash onset to limit spread

exam.step: Palpate behind the ears and at the back of the neck for swollen glands
exam.positive: Postauricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy is a genuine distinguishing feature from measles

exam.step: Ask about joint aches, especially in adult women
exam.positive: A real, commonly-taught feature of rubella, more prominent than in most other childhood exanthems

exam.step: Always ask about pregnancy status, in the patient or a close contact
exam.positive: First-trimester infection risks congenital rubella syndrome -- this changes the urgency of the assessment, even though the illness itself is usually mild

labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis, particularly important for pregnancy risk assessment and public-health notification
Often sufficient with the classic clinical picture in a non-pregnant, non-exposed context

conditions.name: Rubella

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: A generally milder viral illness than measles -- a fine, pink rash spreading from the face down the body over about 3 days, with mild fever and characteristic postauricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy (swollen glands behind the ears and at the back of the neck), a genuine distinguishing feature from measles. Joint aches are common, especially in adult women. The critical clinical point: infection in the first trimester of pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome (deafness, cataracts, heart defects) in the baby -- any suspected rubella in a pregnant woman or her contacts needs prompt assessment for this reason, not for the mother's own mild illness.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis, supported by rubella IgM/PCR testing
Notify public health -- rubella is a notifiable disease in most jurisdictions
Urgent assessment if a pregnant woman is exposed or affected, because of congenital rubella syndrome risk to the baby
Supportive care (fluids, antipyretics) -- the illness itself is usually mild and self-limiting

exam.step: Inspect for grouped, fluid-filled blisters progressing to shallow, painful ulcers in the genital area
exam.positive: The classic appearance -- deliberately compared with Shingles's dermatomal vesicles already modelled in this bundle, though herpes is not confined to a single dermatome

exam.step: Ask whether this is a first episode or a recurrence, and about any fever/flu-like symptoms
exam.positive: First episodes are typically more severe and more likely to have systemic symptoms than recurrences

exam.step: Take a sexual history and discuss partner disclosure
exam.positive: Relevant for risk-factor assessment and for the ongoing management conversation, though no dedicated evidence node captures sexual history directly in this bundle

labs.confirms: Often sufficient given the characteristic appearance

labs.test: Viral PCR or culture of a lesion swab
labs.confirms: Confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2 when uncertain

conditions.name: Genital herpes

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Arrange an appointment in the next day or two

conditions.summary: A common sexually transmitted viral infection causing painful, grouped, fluid-filled blisters that break down into shallow ulcers, typically in the genital area. A first episode is often the most severe, sometimes with fever and flu-like symptoms; recurrences are usually milder and shorter. This is a lifelong infection (the virus remains dormant between outbreaks) -- an important point for a first diagnosis conversation, alongside the fact that outbreaks typically become less frequent and severe over time with appropriate management.
workup: Usually a clinical diagnosis on the characteristic grouped vesicles/ulcers, confirmed with viral PCR/culture of a swab if uncertain
Oral antiviral (aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir) for the first episode -- most effective if started early
Suppressive daily antiviral therapy for people with frequent recurrences, or to reduce transmission risk to a partner
Discuss disclosure and transmission-risk-reduction with sexual partner(s)

exam.step: Ask specifically whether the rash itches
exam.positive: Syphilis's rash is classically NON-itchy -- a genuine, clinically-taught negative discriminator against nearly every other rash-producing condition

exam.step: Inspect the palms and soles specifically
exam.positive: Involvement here is a distinctive, easily-overlooked feature of secondary syphilis

exam.step: Ask about a preceding painless genital ulcer weeks earlier, and check for generalised lymphadenopathy and mucous patches
exam.positive: The classic sequence -- primary chancre followed weeks later by the secondary-stage rash -- though no dedicated evidence node captures the primary chancre directly here

labs.confirms: Used for both initial screening and monitoring treatment response over time
Confirms the diagnosis, remaining positive for life even after successful treatment

conditions.name: Syphilis

triage.label: Urgent
triage.action: Seek medical assessment today

conditions.summary: A sexually transmitted bacterial infection progressing through distinct stages. This models the SECONDARY stage specifically -- a widespread, classically NON-ITCHY rash (often including the palms and soles, a genuinely distinctive feature), sometimes with fever, generalised lymphadenopathy and mucous patches, appearing weeks after an initial, often-painless genital ulcer (the primary chancre, for which no dedicated evidence node exists here -- a disclosed gap). Untreated syphilis progresses through further stages with serious long-term complications, which is exactly why prompt diagnosis and treatment genuinely matter, not just symptom relief.
workup: Serological testing (treponemal and non-treponemal tests) -- the standard diagnostic approach
A single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G for early syphilis -- highly effective and still first-line
Partner notification and testing -- essential given ongoing transmission risk
HIV testing at the same visit -- co-infection is genuinely common and both need addressing
Follow-up serology to confirm treatment response

exam.step: Inspect the distribution -- confined to the diaper area, sparing the skin folds typically
exam.positive: The genuine hallmark, distinguishing simple irritant diaper rash from a more widespread skin condition

exam.step: Look for a beefy-red rash with satellite spots beyond the main rash margin
exam.positive: Suggests a secondary candidal infection, genuinely common and needing topical antifungal treatment

exam.step: Ask specifically about fever or feeling generally unwell, looking for their ABSENCE
exam.positive: Diaper rash is a purely local irritation -- systemic symptoms should prompt considering a different cause instead

labs.confirms: Usually entirely sufficient for diagnosis

labs.test: Referral for a persistent or unusual rash not responding to standard measures
labs.confirms: For atypical presentations needing specialist assessment

conditions.name: Diaper rash

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Irritant contact dermatitis in the diaper area, caused by prolonged skin contact with urine and stool -- genuinely one of the most common skin conditions in infants, peaking around 9-12 months of age. Distinct from the systemic/infective rash conditions sharing this large bundle (measles, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, meningococcal rash): diaper rash is a purely local, non-systemic irritation, without fever, generalised lymph node swelling, or joint involvement.
workup: Frequent diaper changes, gentle cleansing, and generous use of a barrier cream (zinc oxide or petrolatum-based) at every change
Allow nappy-free time to let the skin air-dry where practical

Topical antifungal cream if the rash has the typical appearance of a secondary candidal infection (beefy-red with satellite spots), which is genuinely common if a straightforward rash doesn't settle within a few days
Mild topical steroid for short-term use if inflammation is significant and not settling with barrier measures alone

exam.step: Inspect the distribution -- central face (cheeks, nose, forehead, chin), sparing the periphery typically
exam.positive: The genuine characteristic distribution of rosacea

exam.step: Ask about burning/flushing sensation rather than itch, looking for itch's relative ABSENCE
exam.positive: A genuine distinguishing feature from the itchy rash conditions (eczema, contact dermatitis) sharing this bundle

exam.step: Ask about known triggers and confirm the chronic, adult-onset nature
exam.positive: Rosacea is genuinely rare in children -- a childhood facial rash points toward a different cause instead

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient for diagnosis based on the characteristic distribution and trigger pattern

labs.test: Referral to dermatology for atypical presentations or ocular involvement
labs.confirms: For cases needing specialist assessment, particularly if the eyes are affected

conditions.name: Rosacea

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: A chronic facial skin condition causing persistent redness, flushing, and sometimes small red bumps, typically affecting the central face (cheeks, nose, forehead, chin) -- genuinely common in adults, often triggered by heat, spicy food, alcohol, or sun exposure. Distinct from the eczema/psoriasis/contact dermatitis conditions sharing this bundle: rosacea is characteristically a burning/flushing sensation rather than itch, and is genuinely rare in children.
workup: Ask about known triggers (heat, spicy food, alcohol, sun exposure, stress) and whether flushing precedes the persistent redness
Sun protection and trigger avoidance as a genuinely effective first-line measure for many people
Topical treatment (metronidazole, azelaic acid) for mild-moderate inflammatory rosacea
Oral antibiotics (low-dose doxycycline, used for its anti-inflammatory rather than antibiotic effect) for more significant inflammatory rosacea, under medical guidance

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Widespread rash with breathing difficulty
redFlags.message: Hives together with breathing trouble, facial swelling or faintness is a whole-body allergic reaction.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Spreading skin infection with fever
redFlags.message: A hot red area of skin that is spreading, with fever, needs antibiotics started promptly.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Mark the edge of the redness with a pen so spread can be judged.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
